title: Not the sensor
setting: An engineer refuses to replace a part for the fifth time.

lines.t: Same fault again. Just swap the sensor and get the line running.
That's the fifth sensor this week. I'd like two hours instead.
Downtime costs nine hundred an hour.
And we've paid that four times already for a part that isn't broken.
You think the sensors are fine?
I think they're reporting a real problem accurately.
All right. What's your plan?
Shut down properly, lock out, and look at everything around the sensor.
Two hours. Then we do it your way or mine.
Fair. If I'm wrong, I'll fit the fifth sensor myself.

title: Handover on the twelfth
setting: A client engineer refuses to sign off with 63 items open.

lines.t: We're ready for handover on the twelfth as agreed.
The punch list still has sixty-three items.
All small. Sealant, paint, two door handles.
I know. And after handover, nobody is on site to fix them.
We'd come back.
Sixty-three becomes forty in a month and stays there for a year.
So what are you proposing?
Work the weekend, clear the list below ten, and hand over on the fifteenth.
Three days late.
In writing, agreed by the client, with the as-built drawings complete.

title: Half a millimetre
setting: Parts have arrived built to a drawing that was replaced in March.

lines.t: The specification says 40 millimetres, plus or minus nought point one.
And the parts that arrived?
Half a millimetre out. Outside tolerance on every single one.
Check which drawing they worked from.
That's the problem. They used the blueprint from the prototype.
Which dimension changed between the two?
The mounting hole. It moved when we made the frame load-bearing.
So they built to a drawing we superseded in March.
Our number was on both versions. That part is ours to fix.
One drawing number, one version, and the old one goes in the bin today.
I'll redo the feasibility study for the second frame while we're here, because the same mistake is waiting in it.

title: The machine that sets the pace
setting: The line has to produce more and one machine decides everything.

lines.t: We need to scale up to 900 units a month.
The line does 640 in a good week.
Where's the bottleneck?
The paint booth. Everything before it waits and everything after it starves.
So throughput is decided by one machine.
It always is. A second booth costs 60,000 and eleven weeks of lead time.
And the yield?
94%. Almost every failure traces back to one component supplier.
Which batch?
Everything from June. I've quarantined what's left of it.
Then order the booth, change the supplier, and touch nothing on the assembly line until both are settled.

title: Sunday morning, on purpose
setting: A line that has stopped three times this month.

lines.t: Line two has stopped again. Third time this month.
How much downtime?
Forty minutes today. Two hours last Tuesday.
Have you found the root cause, or are we still guessing?
I've spent two days troubleshooting it. I've ruled out the motor and the sensor.
So which is it?
The belt shows wear and tear beyond its hours. The controller reads fine every time I calibrate it.
Then it's the belt, and the fault has been building for weeks.
I can work around it by running slower until Sunday.
Do that, then shut down the line on Sunday morning and change it properly.
While it's off, I'd overhaul the gearbox as well. It's twelve years old.
Do the overhaul. And if there's a defect in the new belt, I want to hear about it before it's fitted.
Agreed. After this the whole line goes on preventive maintenance, and we retrofit the newer controller in the spring.

title: Eleven items on the list
setting: A new line is nearly finished and the client is counting.

lines.t: We're ready to commission the new line on the 14th.
And the punch list?
Eleven items. Nine of them are paint and labels.
The other two?
A guard that needs moving, and a cable route the subcontractor did his own way.
Then the contractor fixes both before I sign off on anything.
Understood. Can we do the site visit on the 12th?
Bring the as-built drawings. The last project was handed over with drawings from the tender.
These are marked up every week.
Good. And the old line?
We decommission it after two weeks of parallel running, and not a day before.
Then the handover is the 28th, with every item on that list closed.

title: Rust in the wrong place
setting: A frame that has spent six winters outdoors.

lines.t: There's corrosion on the frame near the weld.
How deep?
Surface, so far. It's been outside for six winters.
Which is two winters longer than it was built for.
Is it still safe?
We'll run a stress test before anybody stands on it.
And if it fails?
We replace it. Repeated loading causes fatigue, and fatigue gives no warning before it breaks.
The new one should be a different material.
Something durable outdoors, even at a higher price. This one was chosen for a warehouse and it's been living in a field.

title: One in fifty
setting: The checks find nothing and the customer keeps finding something.

lines.t: Quality control is checking one in fifty.
And finding nothing, which is why nobody wants to change it.
The customer found two faulty units last month.
Out of how many?
Four hundred.
So one in fifty isn't catching it. Go to one in twenty for a month.
That's more hours.
Fewer hours than a recall. And the standard they quote in the contract is stricter than the one we work to.
I'll get a copy of it today.
Read it properly, and back up the test results somewhere other than that one laptop.

title: It could have been his hand
setting: Nobody was hurt, which is exactly why it matters.

lines.t: Somebody reported a near miss on the press yesterday.
Nobody was hurt.
Which is exactly why I want to hear about it today.
He reached in while it was still moving.
Then the hazard is the machine, and the habit is the reason.
He's done it that way for eleven years.
Eleven years of being lucky. Does that press have a lockout?
It has one. Using it costs ninety seconds.
Then ninety seconds is the rule, and I'll say it to everybody myself.
The risk assessment for that area is two years old.
Rewrite it this week, and check that everyone on that line actually wears the PPE we bought in January.
